title: Production and Characterization of Carbide-Free Cast Bainitic Steels with Two Different Mn Contents
abstract: Abstract Carbide-free bainitic steels (Fe–0.8C–1.7Si–0.9Al–1.2Cr–0.2Mo) with two different Mn concentrations (1.4 and 2.0 wt.%) are produced via conventional sand-casting technique. Computational JmatPro calculations were performed to evaluate the present phases and transformation temperatures. Austempering and deep cryogenic heat-treatment are applied. The microstructural, mechanical and wear properties are investigated in detail and compared with those of traditional 100Cr6 bearing steel. With increasing Mn content from 1.4 to 2.0, the  A c 1  and  M s  temperatures decrease and the bainite nose shifts to longer times. The microstructures of studied as-cast bainitic steels are fully pearlitic, whereas the microstructures of austempered steels are composed of bainite and retained austenite. Ultrahigh hardness values (56–59 HRC) are observed for heat-treated steels which are comparable to those for 100Cr6 steels (59–61 HRC for quenched and tempered). Tempered 100Cr6 steels exhibit the best wear resistance with the lowest wear loss. In addition, austempered 1.4Mn and 2.0Mn steels show the best wear resistance among bainitic steels. Their wear resistance is comparable to that of tempered 100Cr6 steels.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: 100Cr6 (SAE52100) grade steel is a high-carbon low-alloyed chromium steel that is utilized in the production of small- and medium-sized bearings due to its high strength, high hardness, superior wear resistance, high-dimensional stability under temperature changes and endurance to contact stress. 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4  Although conventional 100Cr6 bearing steel is the most extensively used metal in the bearing industry, it still has many disadvantages including low fracture toughness, high hydrogen embrittlement susceptibility, and generation of residual tensile stress after heat-treatment. 1 , 4  These disadvantages shorten the service life of bearings working under impact loading conditions and harmful environments. 5  On the other hand, lower bainitic steels obtained through appropriate austempering heat-treatment have recently attracted considerable attention as promising materials for bearing applications. 1 , 6 , 7  Compared with tempered martensitic microstructures of similar hardness, lower bainitic microstructures generally exhibit superior toughness and may also provide improved wear resistance due to their favorable combination of strength, toughness, and retained austenite stability. The fatigue resistance of the lower bainitic microstructure is also better. The residual compressive stress is present on the surface of the lower bainitic parts, which can decelerate the crack propagation. 8 , 9

In addition, the stress on the fatigue crack tip can be released efficiently due to the presence of retained austenite in the bainitic steel microstructure. 10  However, a relatively low austempering temperature (just higher than  M s ) should be essential to form a lower bainitic microstructure and achieve a high hardness/strength. Thus, the bainitic transformation kinetics is slow and a long austempering time is required for formation of lower bainitic microstructure. 9 , 11 ,  12 – 13  Transformation kinetics of steels during cooling is affected by several parameters. The most critical parameters are the chemical composition (C content, type and content of alloying elements) and cooling rate of the steels. In the present study, it is to compare the microstructures, mechanical properties and wear performance of conventional 100Cr6 steel and cast bainitic steels containing two different Mn contents.

Contrary to previous studies that focus on either conventional bearing steels or bainitic steels independently, the present study provides a comprehensive comparison between 100Cr6 bearing steels and Mn-modified cast bainitic steels. The combined analysis of transformation kinetics, retained austenite stability, mechanical properties and wear resistance offers new insights into the design of bainitic steels with improved performance under severe operating conditions .

sections.heading: 100Cr6 Bearing Steel
paragraphs: The conventional 100Cr6 steel used in the present study was received in the spherodized-annealed condition. Its chemical composition is determined using Thermo Fischer Scientific Arl Easy Spark Metal Analyzer model optical spectrometer (OES) and is given in Table  1 . The following heat-treatment is applied to the 100Cr6 steel: (i) austenitizing at 880°C for 120 minutes, (ii) oil-quenching to 60 °C, and (iii) tempering at 180 °C and 235 °C for 90 min. sections.heading: Bainitic Steel
paragraphs: The chemical compositions of the two bainitic steels are given in Table  2 . The steels are produced by a conventional sand-casting technique. The casting is conducted using an Inductotherm medium frequency induction furnace with a capacity of 500 kg at Kulvar Döküm Foundry (Konya, Turkey) and then poured into the standard U blocks. Carbon, ferro-silicon, ferro-manganese, ferro-molybdenum, ferro-chromium, aluminum and steel scrap are used as the furnace charge. After casting the standard U blocks are left to cool for 7 h in sand molds. Then, the casting is fettled, the feeders and sprues are removed and finally sandblasted to obtain a clean surface. Prior to the heat-treatment process, dilatometer tests are conducted to determine the  A c 1  (austenite start) and  A cm  (austenite finish) transformation temperatures. A Linseis L75 model dilatometer is used for the tests. Cylindrical test specimens with 4 mm height and 10 mm diameter are utilized for the dilatometer tests. In addition, the  A c 1 ,  A cm  and martensite start ( M s ) temperatures are also predicted by continuous-cooling-transformation (CCT) and time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagrams calculated by JMatPro software.

The applied heat-treatment processes for cast steels are summarized in Table  3 . All the samples are austenized at 920 °C for 120 min, and then austempered at 250 °C (above the  M s  temperature) for 100 min. Austempering is carried out in a temperature-controlled salt bath containing 50 % NaNO 3  and 50% KNO 3  salt. 14  After austempering heat-treatment, all specimens are left to air-cool. Moreover, some of the austempered samples are subjected to cryogenic heat-treatment. The specimens are left in liquid nitrogen for 18 h and then tempered at 250 °C for 2 h. sections.heading: Characterization
paragraphs: The microstructural characterization of all studied steels is conducted using a Zeiss Gemini 500 model field emission gun scanning electron microscope (FESEM) equipped with an EDS detector. Prior to microstructural investigation, disk specimens (30 mm diameter, 10 mm height) are ground (180–1200 grit), polished (1 μm diamond suspension) and etched (2% nital solution). X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements are conducted to identify the constituent phases. XRD analyses are performed utilizing a Bruker D8 model diffractometer with Cu–K α  source ( λ  = 1.5406 Å). XRD patterns are recorded in the 2 θ  range of 30–100° with a scanning speed of 2°/min.

Rockwell-C hardness test is performed using a Mutitoyo HR-530 model hardness tester. The hardness tests are performed with a 150 kg load and a dwell time of 15 s on polished surfaces. At least seven independent measurements are performed and then averaged. The tensile tests are carried out on a Zwick Roell 8594 model universal testing machine with a strain rate and a capacity of 0.5 mm/min and 250 kN, respectively. The standard tensile test specimens are prepared according to ASTM E8/E8M (Standard Test Methods for Tension Testing of Metallic Materials) standard. Charpy impact tests are conducted using a Hardway Jbs 300B model impact tester according to DIN EN ISO 148-1 (Metallic materials-Charpy pendulum impact test) standard. V-shaped notch standard specimens with 10 × 10 × 55 mm are used in the impact tests. For tensile and impact tests, three identical specimens are tested for each condition.

Sliding wear tests of studied steels are performed utilizing a UTS Tribolog multi-functional tribometer in dry sliding reciprocating mode at room temperature according to ASTM G-133 (Standard Test Method for Linearly Reciprocating Ball-on-Flat Sliding Wear) standard. WC balls with a diameter of 6 mm are used as abrasive balls. Sliding wear tests are often used for tribological comparison. The coefficient of friction and wear volume loss can be determined, and worn-surface analysis can be performed under controlled sliding conditions. Wear tests are performed under 10 N load for 100 m sliding distance. The frequency is 5 Hz and the stroke length is 10 mm. During the wear tests, the friction force and friction coefficient are recorded. Three identical specimens are tested for each condition. The surface profile of the worn surfaces is examined by NanoMap LS 500 model stylus profilometer. The worn surfaces are also analyzed by Nikon MA200 model optical microscope.

sections.heading: 100Cr6 Bearing Steel
paragraphs: The SEM micrographs of as-received and heat-treated 100Cr6 bearing steels are shown in Figure  1 . The microstructure of the as-received specimen (Figure  1 (a)) is composed of spheroidized carbides and a ferrite matrix. As expected, quenched and tempered specimens exhibit martensitic and tempered martensitic microstructures, respectively. However, a minor amount of undissolved carbides is also observed in the microstructures of quenched and tempered specimens. The chemical composition of the carbides for the specimens is also examined with EDS analysis (Table  4 ). The carbides are found to be (Fe, Cr) 3 C with a stoichiometric ratio of about 75:25. Moreover, the XRD analysis (Figure  2 ) of the 100Cr6 samples showed that the diffraction pattern of the as-received sample contains diffraction peaks from  α -Fe (JCPDS Card No: 89-4186) and Fe 3 C (JCPDS Card No: 35-0772) carbide phases. However, the XRD patterns of quenched and tempered samples exhibit diffraction peaks only from the  α -Fe phase. The Fe 3 C phase cannot be observed because of the lower amount than the XRD detection limit. The hardness and tensile test results (Table  5 ) showed that hardness and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) significantly increased after heat-treatment. The spheroidization annealing condition of the as-received sample is the cause of the lower hardness and UTS values. sections.heading: Bainitic Steels
paragraphs: For a specific steel composition, Thermo-Calc software provides estimates of the number and amount of constituent phases as a function of temperature. 15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18  In the case of bainitic steel, the liquidus temperature, the amounts of austenite, pearlite (cementite + ferrite) and the minor phases such as carbides can be determined. The calculated phase diagrams of 1.4 Mn and 2.0 Mn specimens are illustrated in Figure  3 (a) and (b), respectively. The calculations are conducted utilizing a specified standard composition. For both compositions, the major phases are liquid, austenite, cementite and ferrite. Minor phases are M 23 C 6  and M 7 C 3 -type carbides. According to the computed phase diagrams, the ultimate matrix of the studied compositions is composed of cementite, pearlite and a minor amount of other carbides. However, no important differences are observed between the calculated phase diagrams of 1.4 Mn and 2.0 Mn compositions. For high-carbon alloyed steels, the alloying elements can noticeably influence the decomposition of austenite phase during cooling. 19  Therefore, the time-temperature-transformation (TTT) and continuous-cooling-transformation diagrams are calculated utilizing JMatPro software. 20  The predicted TTT and CCT diagrams for both steels are presented in Figures  4  and  5 , respectively. With increasing concentration of Mn from 1.4 to 2.0 Mn, the  A c 1  temperature decreases and  A cm  remains unchanged. In addition, the following conclusions can be drawn from the predicted CCT diagrams (Figure  5 (a) and (b)): With increasing Mn content, (i) the bainite start ( B s ) temperature decreases, (ii) bainite nose shifts to longer times, and (iii) the martensite start ( M s ) temperature decreases. Figure 3 Equilibrium development of phases in (a) 1.4 Mn and (b) 2.0 Mn bainitic steels predicted using JMatPro software. Figure 4 Predicted TTT diagrams of (a) 1.4 Mn and (b) 2.0 Mn bainitic steels. Figure 5 Predicted CCT diagrams of (a) 1.4 Mn and (b) 2.0 Mn bainitic steels.

According to the predicted TTT and CCT diagrams, it is clearly stated that increasing Mn content reduces  A c 1 ,  B s  and  M s  temperatures, and decelerates the bainite formation. Mn is a strong austenite stabilizer and increases the hardenability of steel. By stabilizing austenite, it lowers the thermodynamic driving force for its decomposition into bainite or martensite. 21  As a result, the  B s  and  M s  decrease and the bainite reaction shifts to longer times on TTT/CCT diagrams. In addition,  Ac 1  also decreases with increasing Mn content. Mn makes austenite thermodynamically more stable, so the transformation from ferrite/pearlite to austenite starts at a lower temperature during heating. On the other hand, critical transformation temperatures are also determined with dilatometric analyses (Figure  6 ) and the obtained results are compared with thermodynamic calculations. The  M s  temperature cannot be determined with dilatometric analyses due to the low temperature sensitivity of the equipment at relatively low temperatures. The calculated and measured  A c 1  and  A cm  temperatures (Table  6 ) are consistent with each other. Figure 6 Heating and cooling dilatometric curves for 1.4 Mn and 2.0 Mn bainitic steels. Table 6 Calculated and Measured A c1  and A cm  Temperatures for 1.4 Mn and 2.0 Mn Bainitic Steels Steel Method A c1  (°C) A cm  (°C) 1.4 Mn J Mat Pro 793.8 821.5 Dilatometer 801 826 2.0 Mn J Mat Pro 785.6 821.7 Dilatometer 791 812

The annealing conditions of bainitic steels are determined according to the measured and calculated transformation temperatures. The initial microstructures of bainitic steels in the as-cast state are shown in Figure  7 . Both compositions have a fully pearlitic microstructure in the as-cast state. Since the studied compositions are close to the eutectoid composition, a pearlitic microstructure without the formation of proeutectoid phases is observed. The pearlitic microstructure is also predicted in the calculated phase evolution in Figure  3 . Based on the predictions, the final microstructure of bainitic steels is mostly composed of a pearlite (cementite + ferrite) phase mixture. Figure 7 The SEM micrographs of studied bainitic steels: (a) cast, (b) austempered (1000X), and (c) austempered (10000X).

The cast steels are subjected to austempering heat-treatment to obtain a bainitic microstructure. The microstructures of austempered specimen are shown in Figure  7 (c) and (d). After austempering heat-treatment, the pearlitic microstructure transforms into a microstructure of bainite and residual austenite. The resultant microstructure can be identified as carbide-free bainitic microstructure. Broadly speaking, the morphology of carbide-free bainite is almost like the upper bainite. The only difference is the appearance of retained austenite instead of carbides. In the carbide-free bainitic microstructure, the morphology of retained austenite is in the form of either film-like interwoven between the ferrite plates or blocky-morphology positioned between the bainitic microstructure. The film-like and blocky-morphology retained austenite have different C concentrations: blocky-morphology is much poorer in C than the film-like. The C concentration of two different morphologies of retained austenite mostly depends on two factors: (i) chemical composition of the steel, and (ii) kinetics of bainitic transformation. 21 ,  22 – 23  For the microstructures of studied austempered specimens, retained austenite has a blocky morphology. 1.4 Mn–A and 2.0 Mn–A specimens exhibit similar microstructural features. The only apparent difference is the amount of retained austenite, which is a bit higher for 2.0 Mn-A composition. The volume fractions of bainite and retained austenite are calculated using ImageJ software. The fraction of retained austenite for 1.4 Mn-A and 2.0 Mn–A specimens are calculated as 12.3 ± 0.4% and 18.7 ± 0.5%, respectively. Mn is a significant austenite stabilizer. Therefore, increasing the Mn content results in an increase in the amount of retained austenite. 24

The presence of retained austenite is also confirmed by XRD analyses (Figure  8 ). In the XRD patterns of austempered specimens; (200), (220) and (310) diffraction lines corresponding to the  γ Fe (austenite, JCPDS Card No: 31-0619) are present in addition to the diffraction lines of  α -Fe (ferrite, JCPDS Card No: 89-4186). Figure 8 The XRD patterns of studied bainitic steels: (a) as-cast, (b) austempered and (c) detailed pattern of 1.4Mn-A showing the retained austenite (γ) peaks.

The mechanical properties of bainitic steels in the as-cast state and heat-treated conditions are investigated and compared to those for 100Cr6 bearing steel. Rockwell-C hardness measurements are performed on each specimen, and the results are listed in Table  7 . Austempering leads to a critical increase in hardness values (nearly 1.6–1.7 times). The mean hardness value of the 2.0 Mn composition is moderately higher in the as-cast and austempered conditions. In addition, the following comparisons can be drawn between the results of hardness measurements of bainitic steels and 100Cr6 bearing steel: (i) the hardness of as-cast bainitic steels is much higher than that of spheroidized 100Cr6 bearing steel, (ii) compared to austempered bainitic steels, 100Cr6 bearing steel exhibits much higher hardness in the quenched and 180 °C-tempered conditions, (iii) austempered bainitic steels and 235 °C-tempered 100Cr6 bearing steel exhibit similar hardness values. Table 7 The Rockwell-C Hardness Values of Studied Bainitic Steels Composition Rockwell-C Hardness (HRC) As-cast Austempered DCT DCT-tempered 1.4 Mn 34.8 ± 1.3 56.6 ± 2.2 66.4 ± 2.6 59.8 ± 2.3 2.0 Mn 35.2 ± 1.2 59.4 ± 2.3 61.7 ± 2.4 58.2 ± 2.3

Additionally, deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) is applied to austempered bainitic steels to enhance the microstructural and mechanical properties. 25 , 26  Previous studies stated that sufficient ductility is attributed to the good deformation hardening capability provided by the stress and strain partition between retained austenite and bainite in addition to the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) behavior of the retained austenite. 27 , 28  Although the TRIP behavior of the retained austenite seems to be effective for the ductility, retained austenite can transform to martensite during deformation. The hard and brittle martensite enhances the strain inhomogeneity and incompatibility, increases the crack initiation sites and propagates through the bainite-martensite interface. Thus, formation of martensite results in early fracture and worsens the fatigue resistance and impact toughness. 29 ,  30 ,  31 ,  32 – 33  DCT is a famous treatment to extend the service time of the steel due to the annihilation of retained austenite and the improved yield strength. 34 ,  35 ,  36 ,  37 ,  38 – 39  The microstructures of DCT-tempered steels are illustrated in Figure  9 . The retained austenite transforms to fine martensite laths because of DCT. During DCT retained austenite transforms into martensite rather than bainite because of the large driving force. 40  In addition, carbide particles are detected in the microstructure of 1.4 Mn–DCT specimen. The formation of fine carbide particles during DCT can be explained by following reasons: firstly, transformation of retained austenite to martensite results in a lattice contraction. Therefore, C atoms are forced to diffuse, and a fresh carbide nucleus is formed. Secondly, C-enriched defects can be formed, which are the nuclei of new carbides. These C-enriched defects contain substitutional solute elements, such as Cr, Mo, Mn and Ti, which can also act as effective nucleation sites of carbides. 41 , 42  The measured hardness values (Table  7 ) reveal that the DCT increases the hardness of both compositions. Bensely et al. 43  stated that the enhancement of hardness can be ascribed to: (i) transformation of retained austenite to hard and brittle martensite, (ii) formation of carbide particles, and (iii) combination of previous parameters. The hardness results also indicate the mean hardness value of the 1.4 Mn–DCT specimen is somewhat higher than that of 2.0 Mn–DCT specimen. As the Ms temperature decreases with increasing Mn concentration, the amount of retained austenite is higher for 2.0 Mn composition. Therefore, a relatively small amount of retained austenite transforms to martensite during DCT. A higher amount of martensite and the formation of hard carbide particles are the major reasons for the extremely high hardness values of 1.4 Mn steel after the DCT process. Because of the extremely high hardness of DCT specimens, post-tempering treatment is performed at 235 °C for 90 minutes in order to increase toughness and decrease brittleness. After tempering tempered martensite is present instead of martensite and hardness values are somewhat decreased. Figure 9 The SEM micrographs of DCT-tempered bainitic steels: (a) 1.4 Mn–DCT and (b) 2.0 Mn–DCT.

sections.heading: Wear Properties
paragraphs: Figures  10  and  11  show the wear volume profiles of the acquired wear scars along with 2D profilometric images of all studied 100Cr6 and bainitic steel specimens, respectively. The mean volume loss values for 100Cr6 and bainitic steel specimens are also presented in Figure  12 . For 100Cr6 steel, the 100Cr6–S specimen (as-received spheroidized specimen) exhibits the highest wear loss with the longest and deepest wear scar. The wear loss is somewhat decreased for the quenched condition due to the formation of the hard and brittle martensite phase because of rapid cooling. In addition, tempered 100Cr6 steels exhibit the best wear resistance with the lowest wear loss values (narrowest and shallowest wear scars). The extremely improved wear resistance after tempering heat-treatment is directly attributed to the formation of tougher tempered martensite. Figure 10 The 2D profiles of the wear tracks and optical micrographs of worn surfaces for studied 100Cr6 steels; (a) 100Cr6–S, (b) 100Cr6–Q, (c) 100Cr6–Q–180T and (d) 100Cr6–Q–235T. Figure 11 The 2D profiles of the wear tracks and optical micrographs of worn surfaces for studied bainitic steels; (a) 1.4 Mn–C, (b) 2.0 Mn–C, (c) 1.4 Mn–A, (d) 2.0 Mn–A, (e) 1.4 Mn–DCT and (f) 2.0 Mn–DCT. Figure 12 The calculated wear loss values for studied steels.

For bainitic steels, the cast specimens show the worst wear resistance with highest loss, even worse than as-received 100Cr6–S steel. Contrary to cast bainitic steels, austempered and DCT-tempered specimens show excellent wear resistance like quenched and tempered 100Cr6 steels. For austempered and DCT-tempered conditions, 1.4Mn bainitic steels exhibit better wear resistance than that of 2.0Mn bainitic steels. The wear resistance of bainitic steels commonly depends on their microstructures and resultant mechanical properties. The microstructures of as-cast bainitic steels are pearlite, composed of alternating lamellae of cementite and ferrite. Pearlitic microstructure is relatively heterogeneous and anisotropic. In addition, the hardness of pearlite is considerably lower than that of bainite or martensite. Although hard cementite lamellae provide local reinforcement and the ferrite phase promotes adhesion and plastic smearing, lamellar cracking and fragmentation can occur under cyclic loading. Thus, cast bainitic steels show the lowest wear resistance among the investigated conditions. The bainitic microstructure with fine ferrite laths/plates of austempered bainitic steels is more homogenous than the pearlitic microstructure. The balance between hardness and toughness can suppress crack initiation, and bainite shows superior resistance to crack propagation than pearlite. 44 ,  45 – 46  Therefore, austempered bainitic steels exhibit superior wear resistance compared to cast steels. Moreover, the microstructures of austempered 1.4 Mn and 2.0 Mn steels contain some amount of retained austenite besides bainite. The presence of retained austenite can cause the TRIP effect, which may further enhance wear resistance. This situation seems to be the main reason of superior wear resistance of austempered 1.4Mn and 2.0Mn steels among the investigated bainitic steels. On the other hand, extremely hard and brittle martensite shows resistance to micro-cutting and plowing. However, spalling or micro-cracking can be observed if the brittle martensite is not tempered.

In addition, the variation in friction coefficients for all processed 100Cr6 and bainitic steel specimens is analyzed and shown in Table  8 . Based on the measured friction coefficients, 100Cr6 specimens in spheroidized and quenched conditions exhibit relatively higher friction coefficients compared to those of tempered specimens. 100Cr6 specimens having relatively higher coefficient of friction values (100Cr6–S and 100Cr6–Q) exhibit considerably worse wear resistance with relatively higher wear loss. Similar trends are observed for bainitic steels. Bainitic steels showing importantly higher wear loss like 1.4Mn–C, 2.0Mn–C and 2.0MnDCT have relatively higher coefficient of friction values compared to other bainitic steels showing lower wear loss. Another interesting result is that the coefficient of friction values for 1.4Mn composition are relatively lower than those for 2.0Mn composition. It is clear that 1.4Mn composition exhibits lower wear loss (better wear resistance) than 2.0Mn composition. Table 8 The Coefficient of Friction Values for Studied Steels Steel COF Steel COF 100Cr6–S 0.61 ± 0.06 2.0Mn–C 0.64 ± 0.05 100Cr6–Q 0.76 ± 0.07 1.4Mn–A 0.56 ± 0.05 100Cr6–Q–180T 0.58 ± 0.05 2.0Mn–A– 0.60 ± 0.06 100Cr6–Q–235T 0.56 ± 0.05 1.4Mn–A–DCT 0.57 ± 0.06 1.4Mn–C 0.63 ± 0.06 2.0Mn–A–DCT 0.66 ± 0.07

As a comparison traditional 100Cr6 steel is simpler and more standardized industrially. The studied bainitic steels are more sensitive to heat-treatment parameters, transformation kinetics, chemical composition and retained austenite fraction. It can be concluded that 100Cr6 usually exhibits the highest hardness and often the best wear resistance, especially in the properly quenched and tempered condition. Bainitic steels can approach this performance, but they do not always exceed 100Cr6 unless the microstructure is carefully optimized.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this study, carbide-free bainitic steels are produced via the conventional sand-casting method. The structural, mechanical and wear properties are investigated in detail for cast, austempered and deep-cryogenic-treated (DCT) conditions. The resultant properties are compared with those for 100Cr6 bearing steel. The main findings are summarized as follows: For bainitic steels, with increasing Mn content from 1.4 to 2.0, the A c1  and M s  transformation temperatures decrease and bainite nose shifts to longer times. The microstructures of austempered bainitic steels consist of bainite and retained austenite. The retained austenite transforms to tempered martensite after DCT-tempering. The austempered bainitic steels have high hardness values (56.6–59.4 HRC) comparable to those of tempered 100Cr6 steel (59.1–61.3 HRC), while the DCT-tempered bainitic steels also maintain similarly high hardness levels (58.2–59.8 HRC). Among studied 100Cr6 and bainitic steels, 100Cr6–Q–180T steel exhibits the best wear resistance with the lowest wear loss (0.06 mm 3 ). However, both austempered (1.4Mn-A: 0.13 mm 3  volume loss) and DCT-tempered bainitic steels (1.4Mn-A-DCT: 0.12 mm 3  volume loss) showed significantly improved wear resistance.

Overall, the results indicate that although 100Cr6 still provides superior wear performance, the studied bainitic steels, particularly in the austempered and DCT-tempered conditions, offer a promising combination of high hardness and competitive wear resistance.
